subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 00min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter — Listening to the Poem Aloud

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students to look at the title and the first illustration in the textbook and share, in one sentence each, what they think the poem might be about. This orients attention before the poem is heard.
The teacher reads the entire poem aloud expressively at least twice, pointing to the lines in the textbook. Students follow silently in their books on pp. 1–2, tracking each line with a finger.
The teacher reads stanza by stanza, pausing after each stanza to ask a brief oral question: what picture does this stanza paint? Students call out words or short phrases; no writing yet.
The class attempts a first choral reading of the full poem together, led by the teacher. The teacher models the rhythm; students join in, giving particular attention to the rhyming line-endings.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's chant-like rhyme scheme (tall/fall, sing/anything, share/there, near/cheer, one/begun) naturally supports a strong rhythmic read-aloud; exaggerate the end-rhymes to help students feel the pattern before analysing it. A common pitfall at this stage is rushing through all stanzas without pause — the four brief oral stops between stanzas keep every student anchored to meaning as well as sound.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.2): answer questions on joined hands and helping each other.

periods.activity_title: Reading Comprehension — Thinking About the Poem

time_bands.activity: The teacher leads a brisk choral re-recitation of the poem from the textbook, inviting students to read aloud along with her. This refreshes the poem's language before discussion begins.

Let us Think — A. (p.2): the teacher poses the first question — 'What happens when you join hands with your team?' — aloud and invites two or three oral responses before students write their answers in their notebooks in one or two sentences.

Let us Think — A. (p.2): the teacher poses the second question — 'Why is helping each other important?' — following the same pattern: oral discussion first, then written responses in one or two sentences in the notebook.

A few students share their written sentences aloud. The teacher affirms correct responses by echoing key phrases ('Yes — the goal is near when each hand is joined') and gently corrects any answer that strays outside the poem's imagery.

periods.teacher_notes: Having chanted the poem together, students are primed to draw answers from the poem's own lines — encourage them to cite specific images ('joined hands', 'team spirit') in their written answers rather than giving generic replies about friendship. A common pitfall is accepting answers that could apply to any context; redirect students to the poem's closing couplet, where joy is explicitly born from collective effort.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.2): guided discussion on joy, teamwork, and losing a game.

periods.activity_title: Guided Conversation — Sharing Experiences of Teamwork

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the discussion round: she tells students they will take turns sharing their own experiences, just as the poem's voices cheer together. She models a one-sentence personal example — 'I feel joyful when I complete a puzzle with a friend' — so students understand the expected register.

Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.2): the teacher poses the first two prompts — 'What makes you feel joyful?' and 'Can you think of a good activity you can do together with a friend?' — to the class in pairs. Each pair speaks for a brief turn; the teacher circulates and prompts quieter students.

Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.2): the teacher opens the third prompt — 'Have you ever lost a game? How did you feel?' — to a whole-class share. Three or four students respond; the teacher links their answers to the poem's line 'Win or lose, we always share'.

Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.2): the teacher poses the team-leader scenario — 'Imagine you are the team leader and two teammates disagree; what would you do to unite your team again?' — and takes three or four spoken responses, ending with brief whole-class affirmation of the strategies offered.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's line 'Win or lose, we always share' is the natural anchor for the discussion about losing a game; draw students back to it when responses become too abstract. A common pitfall is allowing only confident speakers to respond — use the pair-turn structure in the first two prompts deliberately to give every student a low-stakes speaking opportunity before whole-class sharing.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.2): pair role-play using the Bokali–Darsana conversation frame.

periods.activity_title: Role-Play Conversation — Foods, Festivals and Unity

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the Bokali–Darsana exchange from the textbook aloud: 'Darsana, I love my country. We have different traditions, food, festivals, and languages but we still stand in unity.' / 'Yes! Bokali, together we stand in unity.' Students listen and then repeat the lines chorally once.

The teacher models completing the sentence frame on the board — 'Hello, I am ______. My favourite food is ______. My favourite festival is ______. In this festival, ______.' — filling in her own details to demonstrate the expected length and tone.

Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.2): student pairs rehearse the role-play, taking turns as Bokali and Darsana. Each partner uses the sentence frame to share their own favourite food and festival. The teacher circulates, listening in and prompting students who hesitate.

Three or four pairs perform their exchange for the class. After each pair, the teacher briefly highlights one interesting food or festival detail they mentioned, connecting the diversity of responses to the poem's theme of unity in difference.

periods.teacher_notes: The Bokali–Darsana dialogue embodies the poem's central claim that diverse traditions strengthen collective identity — help students hear this connection when they perform. A common pitfall is students copying each other's food and festival choices; remind them before the rehearsal phase that the goal is to share what is genuinely true for them, which makes the conversation richer.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (pp.3–4): fill in collective nouns for groups of animals, people and things.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes 'a bunch of bananas' on the board and asks students what they notice about the phrase — 'What is 'bunch' doing in this sentence?' She elicits that it names the group, then introduces the term 'collective noun' with two quick oral examples: 'a herd of cows', 'a swarm of bees'.

The teacher displays the word box from Let us Learn — A. (pp.3–4) on the board: choir, pack, grove, herd, swarm, bunch, bouquet. She works through the first two picture-items (a bundle of sticks — done — and a _______ of sheep) aloud with the class, modelling how to look at the picture clue, read the word box, and choose the best fit.

Let us Learn — A. (pp.3–4): students work individually to complete the remaining blanks (wolves, flowers, trees, bees, boys, keys) in their textbooks or notebooks. The teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck to look at the picture carefully before guessing.

Answers are reviewed as a whole class: the teacher calls on individual students to read a completed sentence aloud. After each answer is confirmed, the teacher asks one quick follow-up — for example, 'Can you think of another word that could mean a group of trees?' — to stretch vocabulary.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse 'pack' (wolves) and 'herd' (sheep) because both suggest a group of animals; make the distinction concrete by linking 'pack' to the way wolves move as a tight hunting unit versus the loose grazing cluster of sheep. The collective noun concept ties directly to the poem's imagery of togetherness — a brief reminder that 'the choir sings together' mirrors 'together we stand, strong and tall' helps students feel the thematic link.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (p.5): fill in prepositions of place using the illustrated town map.

periods.activity_title: Prepositions of Place — Reading the Town Map

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a very simple two-building sketch on the board (a school and a park) and asks students to describe where one is in relation to the other. She elicits or introduces the four target words — behind, between, near, in front of — and writes them on the board.

Students open their textbooks to the town map on p.5. The teacher names each labelled place on the map aloud — Hospital, Bank, Post Office, School, Bookstore, Children's Park — and students point to each in their book, confirming they have found it before any written work begins.

Let us Learn — B. (p.5): students complete all four blanks individually, using the map to verify each answer. The teacher reminds them that the word box — behind, between, near, in front of — is their only source; no other prepositions should be used.

The teacher reviews the four answers sentence by sentence, calling on different students each time. For each answer, she asks a brief confirming question — for instance, 'Is the ambulance between those two buildings? Show me on your map' — so students point-verify before closing their books.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked with collective nouns, students are now shifting to relational vocabulary — make this shift explicit by noting that just as a collective noun names how things belong together, a preposition names how things sit in relation to each other. The most frequent error is confusing 'near' and 'in front of' when buildings are close but not directly facing; the map's roads provide the orientation cue, so encourage students to trace the road between buildings before choosing.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (pp.6–7): write short answers describing helping scenes in five pictures.

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students to open their textbooks to pp.6–7 and conducts a quick picture walk — pointing to each of the five scenes in turn and calling on students to name what they see in one word or phrase: 'injured friend', 'classroom', 'old lady', 'art project', 'raised hands'. No writing yet; this primes visual observation.

The teacher models the first scene (Lubang and his injured friend, p.6) aloud: she thinks through the question — 'What is Lubang doing to help his injured friend, and what will they do next?' — and composes a two-sentence answer on the board, using a present-tense and a future-tense sentence. Students watch and suggest words.

Let us Write — A. (pp.6–7): students write their own one-to-two sentence answers for the remaining four scenes independently — Obang/Manya/Tina cleaning the classroom, Anna helping the old lady, Zakir/Gulpreet/Gilashree and the art project, and students raising hands — in their notebooks.

Students pair up and read one answer each to their partner. Each listener gives a single word of feedback — 'clear', 'interesting', 'I would add…' — and writers make a quick revision if needed. The teacher monitors pairs and draws the sitting to a close with brief whole-class sharing of one strong sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: The five picture scenes on pp.6–7 all embody the poem's theme of helping and solidarity; a brief note that 'this is what the poem's joined hands look like in everyday life' links the writing task to the earlier reading and prevents students from treating it as an isolated observation exercise. The most common writing difficulty at this level is producing only a present-tense description with no future-tense follow-through — the modelled sentence on the board should deliberately demonstrate both tenses so students have a template.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Do You Know + Let us Do (pp.7–8): discuss honeybee waggle dance and ant teamwork as models of collective action.

periods.activity_title: Nature's Teamwork — Bees, Ants and the Waggle Dance

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the Do You Know passage aloud from pp.7–8: honeybees use a waggle dance to share the location of flowers, and ants use signals to find food, defend their colony, and build nests. Students listen with books open.

The teacher leads a whole-class discussion with two oral prompts: 'How is the waggle dance similar to what the poem's team does — cheering and sharing together?' and 'What signal do you think ants might use to say 'danger'?' Students respond freely; the teacher notes interesting ideas on the board.

Students work in pairs: each pair chooses either bees or ants and prepares a short three-sentence spoken explanation — what the creature does together, how they communicate, and one way this resembles teamwork among people. Partners practise saying it to each other before the class share-out.

Four pairs share their explanation with the class — two on bees, two on ants. The teacher closes by asking the class to vote by show of hands: 'Which creature do you think is the better team player — bee or ant?' — keeping the tone light and curious rather than competitive.

periods.teacher_notes: The Do You Know passage positions animal teamwork as a real-world mirror of the poem's message; make this connection explicit when students share — 'Just as the poem says joined hands bring the goal near, the waggle dance brings the whole hive to the flowers.' A common difficulty is students summarising the fact without connecting it to the idea of communication; the paired preparation step is designed to push them past pure recall toward a genuine analogy.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis — Togetherness Across Words, Voices and Actions

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites the class to recite the poem ‘Together We Can’ from memory or from the book, chorally. After the recitation, teacher asks: “Which line do you like most and why?” — two or three students respond briefly.

Quick word-game: teacher calls out a category — animals, people, plants — and students race to name the correct collective noun. Examples drawn from the chapter: a swarm, a herd, a pack, a bouquet, a grove, a choir. Students keep score as a team.

Pairs retell the chapter’s journey in four sentences: the poem’s message, one collective noun they remember, one helping scene from the pictures, and one thing they made or talked about. Each pair shares with the pair beside them.

Independent writing: students write two sentences connecting the chapter to their own life — one about a time they worked as part of a team and one about how it felt. Teacher writes the frame: “Once, my team and I ___. It felt ___.”

Teacher closes with a riddle: “I waggle to guide my team, I rhyme when I cheer, I show togetherness when you unfold me — what am I?” (answers: a bee’s dance, the poem, the paper figure). Students call out answers and celebrate the chapter together.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the poem’s themes, the collective-noun and preposition work, the helping scenes, and the nature extension — students who have encountered any part of the chapter will have something to contribute. The closing riddle bundles the three strands of the chapter (poem, word work, craft) into one playful moment of recognition.

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 1 beginning "With each hand joined, the goal is near." What does the poet mean by "the goal is near" when hands are joined?

options.label: A
options.text: A goal can only be scored in a sports match.

options.label: B
options.text: Holding hands stops people from running fast.

options.label: C
options.text: The finishing line of a race is very close by.

options.label: D
options.text: Working together helps people achieve what they want.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student read 'goal' as a literal sports term rather than a shared aim.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals a literal physical reading of 'joined hands' that misses the poem's metaphorical meaning.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Shows the student has not moved beyond the sports context implied by 'win or lose' earlier in the poem.

items.item_stem: Bokali says to Darsana: "We have different traditions, food, festivals, and languages but we still stand in unity." Which of the following best describes what Bokali means?

options.label: A
options.text: Differences in culture make it impossible to be united.

options.label: B
options.text: Only people who eat the same food can be friends.

options.label: C
options.text: Sharing different traditions makes a country's unity richer.

options.label: D
options.text: Speaking the same language is the only way to stand together.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the student has focused on the food detail without grasping the broader unity message.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a misreading of Bokali's statement as a problem rather than a celebration of diversity.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student has latched onto the 'languages' detail and ignored the inclusive thrust of Bokali's words.

items.item_stem: Look at the picture on Textbook page 6 showing Anna helping an old lady. Choose the sentence that best describes what Anna is doing right now.

options.label: A
options.text: Anna is asking the old lady for directions.

options.label: B
options.text: Anna is helping the old lady cross the road.

options.label: C
options.text: Anna is running past the old lady quickly.

options.label: D
options.text: Anna is waving goodbye to the old lady.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student noticed a farewell gesture but did not read the helping action correctly.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals the student interpreted Anna's proximity to the old lady as a conversation rather than physical help.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student has not engaged with the scene's cooperative intent.
